title: How big is Mars?
dadNotes: Mars is about 6,800 km across, about half of Earth's 12,756 km. About two Marses fit across Earth.
Mars gravity is 38 per cent of Earth's, so a jump is about 2.6 times higher there.
The Moon's gravity is about one sixth of Earth's: a 30 cm jump becomes about 1.8 m there, as tall as Dad.
A Mars day is about 40 minutes longer than ours. A Mars year is almost two of ours.
Olympus Mons is about 22 km tall: about two and a half Mount Everests (8.8 km) stacked up.
Mars air is very thin: under 1 per cent of Earth's air pressure.

steps.title: The red planet
steps.text: This is Mars, our next-door neighbour in space. It is a cold, dusty planet that looks rusty red.
steps.wow: About half as wide as Earth!
steps.dad: Ask Finn: could you walk all the way round it in a day?

steps.title: Guess!
steps.prompt: How many Marses would fit across Earth?
steps.reveal: Good guess! About two Marses fit across Earth. Think of Earth as a football, and Mars would be a grapefruit.

steps.title: Planet Lineup and Mars Jump
steps.intro: Tap each planet to see how big it is, then press JUMP to see how high Finn could jump on Mars.

steps.title: A giant volcano
steps.text: On Mars there is a volcano called Olympus Mons. It is about 22 kilometres tall, one of the tallest mountains we know of.
steps.wow: About two and a half Mount Everests stacked up!

steps.title: Guess!
steps.prompt: How long is one year on Mars?
steps.reveal: Good guess! Mars is further from the Sun, so it takes longer to go round. One year on Mars is almost two of our years.

steps.title: A longer day
steps.text: This is a sunset on Mars, seen by a rover. A day on Mars is a little longer than a day on Earth.
steps.wow: About 40 minutes longer, nearly as long as a football half!
steps.dad: Ask Finn: what would you do with 40 extra minutes every day?

steps.title: A helicopter on Mars
steps.why: Watch a tiny helicopter take off and land on Mars, in air that is very thin.

steps.title: Try it at home: The Mars jump test
steps: Finn stands next to the wall and reaches up as high as he can. Dad puts a sticky note where his fingertips reach.
Now Finn jumps as high as he can, touching the wall at the top of his jump.
Dad puts a second sticky note at that top mark. Measure the gap between the two notes. That is Finn's jump on Earth.
Multiply the jump by 2.6. That is how high Finn would jump on Mars.
Multiply the jump by 6. That is how high Finn would jump on the Moon. Is it as tall as Dad?
steps.why: Mars pulls more gently than Earth, and the Moon pulls even less, so you float higher before you come back down.

debrief: Who would fix the toilet on Mars?
